parole.significato: The spontaneous removal of a limb, tail etc, especially by some invertebrates as a self-defense mechanism.
parole.testo: From auto- + -tomy, after German Autotomie or French autotomie.

parole.significato: An alto instrument of the clarinet family, pitched in F below middle C, with a range reaching down to F below that.
parole.testo: From German Bassetthorn, translation of French cor de bassette, from Italian corno di bassetto.

parole.significato: A streaky form of phytophotodermatitis caused by exposure to perfume containing bergapten.
parole.testo: From German Berlocke (“pendant”) or French breloque (“charm, pendant”).

parole.significato: The state of having two male partners.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from German Biandrie or French biandrie. Equivalent to bi- + -andry.

parole.significato: A letterman at Oxford or Cambridge.
parole.testo: From the German surname, Americanized from Blau or its French cognate bleu.

parole.significato: A group of businesses or nations that collude to limit competition within an industry or market.
parole.testo: In the business sense, borrowed from German Kartell, first used by Eugen Richter in 1871 in the Reichstag. parole.significato: A cowhide with the belly and neck removed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Croupon, from French croupon, from Middle French crepon, from Old French crepon, from crope (“buttocks”) + -on.

parole.significato: A shop that sells cooked or prepared food ready for serving.
parole.testo: Attested since 1954. Clipping of delicatessen, from German Delikatessen, plural of Delikatesse (“delicacy, fine food”), from French délicatesse, derived from the adjective délicat, from Latin delicatus.

parole.significato: A shop that sells cooked or prepared foods ready for serving.
parole.testo: First attested 1864. From German Delikatessen, plural of Delikatesse (“delicacy, fine food”), at the time also spelled Delicatesse(n), from French délicatesse, from délicat (“fine”), from Latin delicatus (“alluring”). parole.significato: The state of being sexually and romantically attracted primarily or exclusively to persons of the same sex, sometimes (…
parole.testo: From homosexual + -ity, equivalent to homo- + sexuality and after the model of German Homosexualität, coined by journalist Karl Maria Kertbeny in 1869, and French homosexualité, attested in 1891.

parole.significato: Out of order; not working.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German kaputt (“broken, out of order”), from French capot (“to be without a trick in the card game Piquet”). Cognate to Dutch kapot. Doublet of capot and capote.

parole.significato: A homologous series of organic molecules whose functional group is an oxygen atom joined to a carbon atom—by a double b…
parole.testo: From German Keton, from Aketon (“acetone”), from French acétone (“acetone”). See acetone.

parole.significato: A tendency to take a miserable or pessimistic view on life; a consistently miserable outlook, negativity.
parole.testo: From German Miserabilismus, French misérabilisme, corresponding to miserable + -ism.

parole.significato: Acting or tending to confound, obfuscate, or obscure.
parole.testo: Entering English circa 1793–1799: From German Obskurant and French obscurant, from classical Latin obscūrant-, stem of obscūrāns, present participle of obscūrāre (“to obscure”), from obscūrus (“dark”).

parole.significato: A fish, the ide, Leuciscus idus.
parole.testo: 19th century. Borrowed from German orfe, orf, possibly from French orphe or Old High German orvo, from Latin orphus (“gilt-head bream”), from Ancient Greek ὀρφώς (orphṓs, “sea perch”). May be related to Old English eorp, earp (“dark, dusky”), Old High German erpf (“brown”), Old Norse jarpr (“brown”)

parole.significato: Synonym of Paulist (“a person who follows or is associated with Paul the Apostle or his doctrines.”).
parole.testo: From Latin Paulīnus + -ian, partly after German paulinisch and partly after French paulinien. By surface analysis, Pauline + -ian.

parole.significato: A card game, similar to bezique.
parole.testo: Perhaps from Austro-Bavarian pronunciation of German Binokel (where b>p change is common) , French binocle (literally “pince-nez”), a related card game.

parole.significato: The profound feeling of realizing that everyone, including strangers passing in the street, has a life as complex as on…
parole.testo: Coined by American author and neologist John Koenig in 2012, whose project, The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, aims to come up with new words for emotions that currently lack names. Inspired by German sonder- (“special”) and French sonder (“to probe”).

parole.significato: The grasslands of Eastern Europe and Asia.
parole.testo: From German Steppe or French steppe, in turn from Russian степь (stepʹ, “flat grassy plain”) or Ukrainian степ (step). There is no generally accepted earlier etymology, but there is a speculative Old East Slavic reconstruction *сътепь (sŭtepĭ, “trampled place, flat, bare”), related to топот (topot),

parole.significato: A public sale or auction required by law, especially one in Germany or neighbouring territories.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Subhastation or French subhastation, from Latin subhastātiō, from sub hastā (literally “under the spear”). Compare Spanish subasta (“auction”).

parole.significato: A symbol consisting of three spirals, or three bent human legs.
parole.testo: 1880, via German Triskeles (c. 1850), from French triskèle (1835). It is in turn from Ancient Greek τρισκελής (triskelḗs, “three-legged”), composed of τρι- (tri-, “three”) + σκέλος (skélos, “leg”).

parole.significato: A black liquid used in lithography for drawing and painting and in etching and the silk-screen process as a resist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Tusche, from tuschen, from French toucher.

parole.significato: A thin decorative covering of fine material (usually wood) applied to coarser wood or other material.
parole.testo: From German Furnier, from furnieren (“to inlay, cover with a veneer”), from French fournir (“to furnish, accomplish”), from Middle French fornir, from Old French fornir, furnir (“to furnish”), from Old Frankish frumjan (“to provide”), from Proto-Germanic *frumjaną (“to further, promote”). parole.significato: A mineral occurring in tetragonal crystals, usually of a brown or grey colour and consisting of silica and zirconia.
parole.testo: From German Zirkon, possibly via French zircon, formed in the 1780s from Arabic زَرْقُون (zarqūn), borrowed from Middle Persian zlgwn' (/⁠zargōn⁠/). Doublet of jargoon.
